sources: CCE 1SW Wk1 Day 3 canonical lesson, Super Sports Manufacturing, accessed 2026-08-15.
Find Your Future pp. 204-206, Super Sports Manufacturing.
Private teacher-created AVID source deck, inherited layout and lesson choreography only.
recovery: Use the embedded FYF pages, pre-drawn rack scaffold, and tape or dry-fit route. Hot glue is never required for access; the Canvas Student Guide remains the absence route.

texts:
Super Sports Manufacturing
Design • Build • Test
slides.lookFor: Students enter and leave all glue guns unplugged.
slides.pivot: Hold this cover while materials stay at the supervised stations.

slides.lookFor: Pairs and station routes are visible before the launch.
slides.pivot: Assign pairs from the posted list; do not spend work time negotiating partners.

texts:
Today’s Lesson
Sketch + label
Choose material + weld
Build one rack
Test one weak spot

FYF pp. 204-206
Pencil + ruler
Partner materials stay closed
Tape/dry-fit route available

Discussion

Who designs a bike rack?
Who builds it?
Who checks that it holds up?
slides.lookFor: Students can name the individual sketch and the one shared tested prototype.
slides.pivot: State the no-glue-yet rule before displaying the materials.

images.alt: Find Your Future Super Sports Manufacturing bike-rack design brief

texts:
How many bikes use the rack near our school?

If a district orders 100 new racks, who designs them, who builds them, and what must they survive?

Word Bank:
design     weld     inspect
weather     load     joint
prototype     production
Write one role and one job that role performs.
slides.lookFor: One named role plus a visible task, not just 'factory worker.'
slides.pivot: Offer designer, welder, production technician, and quality inspector as starting roles.

texts: You are the expert welder at SuperSports Manufacturing. The rack must be durable, functional, weather-resistant, and repeatable 100 times.
slides.lookFor: Students understand that one prototype represents a repeatable production decision.
slides.pivot: Ask what changes when a company must build 100 identical products, not one craft project.

texts: Hold multiple bikes without bending. Survive outdoor weather. Fit near sidewalks. Use joints another team could build the same way.
slides.lookFor: Sketch ideas respond to at least three requirements.
slides.pivot: Point to the requirement a decorative idea must still satisfy.

texts:
FYF p. 204
TOP VIEW = from above
SIDE VIEW = from the side

Label where bikes sit and where the rack touches the ground.
slides.lookFor: Both views are present and refer to the same rack shape.
slides.pivot: Use the pre-drawn scaffold; students modify and label rather than start from a blank page.

images.alt: Find Your Future top-view and side-view bike-rack sketch spaces

texts: ALUMINUM — lightweight; no rust; bends and dents • STAINLESS STEEL — very strong; no rust; heavy • CARBON STEEL — strong; affordable; may rust if uncoated
slides.lookFor: One metal choice plus a pro and a tradeoff from the source table.
slides.pivot: Use: I chose ____ because ____, even though ____.

texts: SPOT — small points in thin metal • FILLET — pieces at an angle • SURFACING — fills a hole • CORNER — supports an outside angle
slides.lookFor: Students choose a named method that matches the geometry of the joint.
slides.pivot: Hold two sticks in an L shape and ask which method is designed for that angle.

images.alt: Find Your Future metal tradeoffs and welding-method reference

texts:
Today’s Lesson
Name the weld.
Point to the joint.
Explain why it fits.
Example: Fillet weld here because the upright meets the base at an angle.
slides.lookFor: Every arrow has a weld name; at least one label explains the joint shape.
slides.pivot: If labels say only 'weld here,' return students to the four-method reference.

images.alt: Find Your Future welding-method chart used to label the bike-rack sketch

texts: Partners compare both sketches. Build ONE rack together • Choose the design with clearer requirements and weld labels—not the fastest drawing • Cannot agree? Use the design you can explain and test.
slides.lookFor: Each pair points to one selected sketch and names why it is buildable.
slides.pivot: Teacher assigns the clearer labeled design when a pair remains stuck.

texts:
VOICE 1
Gun stays on the heat-safe mat
Craft gloves before glue
Scraps in the tray
One pair per station
Tape or dry-fit counts equally
slides.lookFor: Students can point to the mat, gloves, scrap tray, timer, and their assigned connection route.
slides.pivot: If station control is not ready, run the entire build as tape/dry-fit; do not delay the design evidence.

images.alt: Find Your Future prototype build and strength-test directions

texts:
One rack.
One visible timer.
One safe route.
Match the chosen sketch. Try more than one joint when a section feels weak.
slides.lookFor: Pairs build the selected geometry, keep materials at stations, and adjust at least one weak connection.
slides.pivot: At minute 39, stop decoration and require a standing base plus one tested joint.

texts: Press gently • Does it balance or wobble? • Name the strongest joint • Name the weak spot • What would you reinforce first?
slides.lookFor: Each pair names one observed weak spot and one evidence-based reinforcement.
slides.pivot: If a rack fails completely, use the failure as the test result; students do not need to rebuild.

texts:
Rank the Three Metals
1 = best outdoors • 2 = middle • 3 = weakest fit
Use one pro and one con for #1. Name the weak prototype joint, the weld that strengthens it, and one other Manufacturing career.
slides.lookFor: The ranking cites the source table, the weak spot matches the prototype test, and the second career has a task.
slides.pivot: Allow labeled bullets and the metal-choice sentence frame.

images.alt: Find Your Future metal pros, cons, and welding-method reference used for the exit ticket

texts: Tomorrow: use case evidence to plan for two robot problems.
slides.lookFor: Sketches are labeled, one prototype per pair is accounted for, and all glue guns are unplugged on mats.
slides.pivot: Students leave prototypes in the named tray; do not spend the final minute on a gallery walk.
